text: Herman cooed. “It’s just a little... observer collar. Nothing too invasive. Think of it as telemetry with perks. It pings. It pricks. It occasionally floods your bloodstream with helpful mood stabilizers. And if you behave... maybe even a treat.” “You’re still free to hunt, of course. Mostly. Just don’t mind the tremors. Or the aim drift. Or the fact that you might forget what you were doing halfway through a chase. It’s all part of the fun. Honestly, you should be grateful. Most specimens don’t get to roam. You’re free-range. Very modern.” Wesker dragged in a breath, chest heaving against the static still caging his ribs. “I will end you.” Herman’s laugh was warm, indulgent. “Oh, I hope so. Otherwise — where’s the fun?” A faint scratch of pen on clipboard followed, his voice dipping into clinical detachment as if Wesker’s rage were nothing more than a lab reading. “Subject 06-W: Successful restraint application. Initial response: extreme hostility. Uroboros activity — suppressed but volatile. Further observation required.” Chapter 2: The First Misfire The Fog unfolded around him, dropping him into the corroded halls of Midwitch. The air smelled of salt, rust, and purpose; steel corridors, slick with condensation, the dull electric hum that meant life. Wesker stepped forward through it, shoulders square, the practiced rhythm of a hunter in his element. Controlled. Familiar. The sting of Herman’s baton, the blackout, the unfamiliar weight at his wrist — all ghosts. Faint echoes. Whatever the Doctor had done, the Fog would bleed it clean. It always had. Here, he was still the killer. Still the apex. He told himself that with every step. And for a few heartbeats, it was even true. A misfired generator flared in the distance. The first chase was a breath away, and he glided toward it, each step clean and confident. Feng darted into view between the pallets, her ponytail snapping like a warning flag. He tracked her automatically — angle, distance, timing. Uroboros surged at his call, pulsing hot and certain through every muscle fiber. He reached for it — And his arm stopped. Not hesitated. Locked. Every muscle from shoulder to wrist seized mid-motion, tendons pulled tight as wire. His lunge faltered, all power diverted into useless momentum. For a split second, his entire system stuttered: vision fractured into white noise, footsteps blurred beneath him. A static heartbeat pounded in his ears. He swiped wide. Feng, shocked for half a breath, twisted out of reach and bolted. Her startled yelp turned into a laugh. It was short, bright, human. Full of the kind of relief that comes with a monster tripping when it should have caught you. She vaulted a pallet and dared a look back. Dared. Wesker's jaw clenched hard enough to ache. He forced movement back into his limbs, teeth grinding as he ripped control back from wherever it had gone. The virus surged in answer, pulsing hot and agitated under the skin — but the pathway it was trying to follow had already been rerouted. Uroboros twisted against the resistance like a living thing but found no foothold. The misfire wasn’t physical. It was command-level. The cuff at his wrist pulsed again — a gentle thrum, almost curious. He caught her eventually. Crushed her to the hook with brutal efficiency, as expected. The hook screamed as it accepted her weight; the Fog purred, sated. But the moment was already gone. The rhythm was wrong. Too slow. Too heavy. Not the clean predator he demanded of himself. As the trial dragged on, the rot set in. A half-second lag on each strike. A stutter in the throws. Muscle memory corrupted. Precision frayed. He felt the precision bleeding out of him with each chase. Somewhere across the map, a locker creaked open. Footsteps danced toward a generator. He followed automatically — but his chest was tight. Not with strain. With uncertainty. He adjusted. He always did. But it wasn’t enough. Every time the cuff warmed against his skin, it left behind a tremor. The next strike came a fraction too slow. The next throw overcorrected. The next lunge landed — but sloppily. A half- second off at every angle. Worse than failure was the realization: he was no longer sure whether the failures were his. Then came the pulse. Mid-trial. No warning. The band warmed gently against the bone, like approval. A pat on the head dripping with condescension. Wesker froze. He was standing in the open. No one nearby. No threat. Nothing to react to. And yet — the cuff had reacted anyways. In the silence between the Fog’s murmurs, a slow coil of unease threaded through him. That pulse had meant something. He was being monitored. Still. Herman was watching. Recording. Adjusting. Chapter 3: Futility The return to his domain was supposed to be automatic, restorative. He should have felt the usual clarity returning, Uroboros smoothing through his veins, mind slotting back into precision. Instead, the stillness of the station almost seemed to hum in a rhythm that matched the pulse under the cuff. Wesker paced like a caged animal, back in the far corner of the RPD station that was supposed to be his. The Fog was quiet here. Too quiet. A stillness that only gave his fury room to breathe and made every joint ache. He dismissed it at first. The body always complained after a hunt. He washed the blood from his gloves, reset the equipment, sat at the edge of a bench and waited for the fatigue to bleed away. It didn’t. The band at his wrist warmed by degrees; barely perceptible at first, then sharp enough to feel like a fever under the skin. He flexed his hand, irritation a slow rise in his throat. Fine. He would catalogue the sensation, adapt. His eyes stayed fixed on the black band clamped to his wrist. The faint hum never stopped.
